questions.stem: A client with severe COPD and chronic hypercapnia has an SpO2 of 84% on room air and increasing lethargy. Which oxygen strategy should the nurse anticipate while ventilation is reassessed?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Titrate controlled oxygen toward an SpO2 of 88% to 92% and promptly reassess ventilation and carbon dioxide status now.","B":"Withhold oxygen because any supplemental oxygen can suppress respiratory drive in a client with chronic hypercapnia.","C":"Use high-concentration oxygen to maintain an SpO2 of 100% and defer ventilation assessment until saturation is normal.","D":"Provide oxygen only during sleep because daytime oxygen increases carbon dioxide retention more than nocturnal therapy in the hospital."}}
questions.rationale: A client with COPD at risk for hypercapnic respiratory failure should not be left hypoxemic. Controlled oxygen is titrated to a target such as 88% to 92%, with prompt reassessment of ventilation and carbon dioxide when mental status is worsening. Oxygen should not be withheld, and routinely targeting 100% can cause excessive oxygen exposure. The rationale is not simply “preserving hypoxic drive”; controlled oxygen and ventilation assessment are the safer clinical framework.
questions.source_name: American Association for Respiratory Care — Oxygen Therapy Clinical Practice Guideline
questions.source_detail: Adult oxygen guidance: COPD target saturation 88%–92%; reassess oxygenation/ventilation clinically

questions.stem: An alert client with diabetes has a blood glucose of 58 mg/dL, shakiness, and can swallow safely. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Administer glucagon immediately and keep the client NPO until the glucose has been normal for at least one hour.","B":"Give a full mixed meal, then wait one hour before rechecking glucose or giving additional hypoglycemia treatment.","C":"Give about 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck the blood glucose in approximately 15 minutes.","D":"Administer IV dextrose despite the client being alert and able to take carbohydrate safely by mouth."}}
questions.rationale: For an alert person who can safely swallow, the ADA recommends fast-acting carbohydrate for hypoglycemia, typically about 15 g for most individuals, followed by glucose reassessment after 15 minutes and repeat treatment if needed. Glucagon or IV glucose is generally reserved for situations in which oral treatment is not feasible or appropriate; waiting an hour delays reassessment.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association — Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026
questions.source_detail: Hypoglycemia Treatment: fast-acting carbohydrate; most individuals 15 g; recheck in 15 minutes

questions.stem: A postoperative client with prolonged immobility suddenly develops pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and an SpO2 of 86%. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assist the client to ambulate to improve venous return while observing whether the symptoms resolve with activity.","B":"Stay with the client, support oxygenation, activate urgent evaluation, and prepare for acute pulmonary embolism workup.","C":"Apply a warm compress to the chest and reassess in 20 minutes because postoperative musculoskeletal pain is more common.","D":"Document the event and notify the next shift if symptoms persist because pulmonary embolism usually develops gradually."}}
questions.rationale: Sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia, recent surgery, and immobility are concerning for acute pulmonary embolism, which requires prompt evaluation and treatment. The nurse should remain with the client, support oxygenation, and escalate urgently. Ambulation, delayed reassessment, or deferring notification can worsen risk and delay care.
questions.source_name: AHA/ACC Multisociety — 2026 Guideline for Acute Pulmonary Embolism
questions.source_detail: 2026 guideline emphasizes prompt diagnosis/treatment; recent surgery and immobility are risk factors

questions.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease has potassium 5.6 mEq/L, no symptoms, stable vital signs, and no known ECG changes. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Administer IV calcium immediately because every potassium value above 5.5 mEq/L requires urgent cardiac membrane stabilization.","B":"Ignore the result because mild hyperkalemia has no cardiac relevance unless potassium exceeds 7.0 mEq/L.","C":"Administer potassium chloride to prevent intracellular potassium depletion caused by chronic kidney disease.","D":"Notify the provider, review medications and renal status, and obtain repeat potassium and ECG assessment as needed."}}
questions.rationale: A potassium of 5.6 mEq/L is hyperkalemia and deserves clinical assessment, medication/renal review, confirmation when appropriate, and ECG evaluation based on context. Immediate IV calcium is used for myocardial stabilization in more dangerous presentations such as significant ECG changes or severe toxicity, not automatically for every mildly elevated value. Potassium replacement is inappropriate, and the result should not be ignored.

questions.stem: A postoperative client is at risk for atelectasis after abdominal surgery. Which nursing plan best supports postoperative lung expansion?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Encourage deep breathing, directed coughing, early mobility, and adequate analgesia; use incentive spirometry as an adjunct.","B":"Use incentive spirometry alone every hour and avoid ambulation until the client can perform the device without discomfort.","C":"Keep the client on bed rest, limit coughing to protect the incision, and increase oxygen only if shortness of breath develops.","D":"Restrict oral fluids and minimize position changes so incisional pain does not interfere with postoperative respiratory effort."}}
questions.rationale: Postoperative pulmonary prevention is multimodal. Deep breathing, directed coughing, early mobilization, and adequate pain control support lung expansion; incentive spirometry may be used as an adjunct but routine incentive spirometry alone is not supported as superior therapy. Bed rest, suppressing cough, and unnecessary fluid restriction do not prevent atelectasis.
questions.source_name: American Association for Respiratory Care — Incentive Spirometry Clinical Practice Guideline
questions.source_detail: Postoperative guidance: incentive spirometry alone is not recommended routinely; combine with deep breathing/coughing, early mobilization and analgesia
